text: Hi, we're team CodeWick. This is AuLens, built for Hack in Hills, powered by TinyFish.
On MCX, gold trades as five futures contracts, and their prices never line up. A Gold Guinea at one lakh thirteen thousand, next to a Gold Ten at one lakh forty thousand, looks like free money.
It isn't. Quote units, purity, settlement city and expiry explain almost all of it.
AuLens converts every contract to one unit, models where each pair must settle, and tests what's left walk-forward, net of modelled costs. One verdict per pair.
Here's the live prototype, on eighteen months of real MCX data.
The scoreboard: six gold and silver pairs. Zero of six establishes an edge.
Take the control pair, Gold Ten against Gold Guinea: sixty-two trades, minus seventeen thousand rupees, break-even at three rupees of slippage. No edge.
The gap settles within one rupee on all eighteen expiries, but only after a trader must exit for delivery.
Check a gap you see: type two prices, and AuLens shows what's left after the rules and costs.
Results are stress-tested for slippage and split by regime.
Alerts fire only for a tested edge. Today, there are none.
Under the hood: MCX settlement data, a rule normalizer, a cost engine and a monthly walk-forward test, in Python and Streamlit.
Gold Ten against Gold Petal made about thirty-five thousand rupees, but fails the verdict's tests: profit in every regime, and a confidence interval above zero.
Limits: fills are simulated, funding costs are excluded, and there's no untouched holdout yet.
Other tools show a gap. AuLens tells you if it's real, and tradable after costs.
It's free for traders, with a Pro tier and an API for brokers.
Next: live bid and ask for measured slippage, then base metals.
AuLens: five contracts, one metal, one honest verdict. It's open source and live today. Thank you.
